lesson.title: One Complex Number, All the Power Information: Complex Power S
lesson.summary: Complex power S = P + jQ packages real power, reactive power, and apparent power into a single complex quantity, computed directly from voltage and current phasors as S = V times the conjugate of I.
lesson.body:
Just as resistance and reactance combine into the single complex number Z = R + jX, and conductance and susceptance combine into Y = G + jB, real power and reactive power combine into a single complex quantity called complex power, S = P + jQ, measured in volt-amperes, VA. Here P is real power, the useful watts computed earlier, and Q is reactive power, the volt-amperes reactive, VAR, that slosh between source and load without being consumed. Writing them together as one complex number is not just tidiness, it lets you use ordinary complex-number algebra, addition, magnitude, and angle, to manage all three power quantities, real, reactive, and apparent, at once.

Complex power is computed directly from phasors: S = Vrms times the complex conjugate of Irms, the RMS voltage phasor multiplied by the complex conjugate of the RMS current phasor. Using the conjugate is what makes the signs come out correctly, positive Q for an inductive, current-lagging, load and negative Q for a capacitive, current-leading, load. There is also a second formula that skips finding voltage separately: S = |Irms|^2 times Z, RMS current squared times the complex load impedance, useful whenever the current and the impedance are already known.

Return to the load Z = 8 + j6 ohms from the impedance triangle example, with |Z| = 10 ohms and angle 36.87 degrees, now fed by a source V = 120 V RMS at angle 0 degrees. The current phasor is I = V/Z = 120 at 0 degrees divided by 10 at 36.87 degrees = 12 A RMS at angle -36.87 degrees. Complex power is S = V times I conjugate = 120 at 0 degrees times 12 at 36.87 degrees = 1440 VA at angle 36.87 degrees. Converting to rectangular form, S = 1440(cos 36.87 + j sin 36.87) = 1440(0.8 + j0.6) = 1152 + j864 VA, so P = 1152 W and Q = 864 VAR. Check this against the second formula: |I|^2 Z = 12^2 times (8 + j6) = 144 times (8 + j6) = 1152 + j864 VA, exactly matching.

Every one of the three headline power numbers falls straight out of this one complex number: the real part, Re(S) = 1152 W, is the real power actually consumed; the imaginary part, Im(S) = 864 VAR, is the reactive power cycling in and out of the load's reactance; and the magnitude, |S| = 1440 VA, is the apparent power the source must be sized to deliver.

That last figure is why complex power shows up on nameplates and datasheets rather than staying a purely academic quantity. Generators, transformers, and circuit breakers are all built to survive a certain current at a certain voltage, and current depends on |S|, not on P alone. A transformer rated 1440 VA can safely supply this exact load, but rating it at 1152 W, the real power alone, would understate the current it must actually carry and risk overheating it. That same triple, P, Q, and |S|, tied together by the Pythagorean theorem exactly the way R, X, and |Z| were, is what the power triangle draws out visually next.
